content:
current status (45 days in)

Other projects are posting their notes, and other people are using my project to feed into theirs, so I've decided to resume posting my progress - just off the main channel. Also it's just nice to have someone to talk to about this stuff. :)

I started working on #Autoformalization > Jacobian challenge on 4/24/2026. Currently origin/main is 2,831 commits deep.

Here is a snapshot of my blueprint dependency graph:

The 12 orange nodes correspond to roughly 18 open sorrows (the link goes to a list of GitHub issues tagged sorry).

Every node in the graph has at least some amount of informal TeX, often with a "Plain English" translation. These are readable in the full blueprint.

Current meta-strategy (scialect)

I started with a Claude session spawning out to Aristotle, but I have since abandoned that approach. I am currently using a swarm of 7-8 TUI agents, usually a mix of:

  • claude code
  • openAI codex
  • google antigravity (the agent, not the IDE)
  • grok build (but it tends to freeze up so i don't use it much at the moment)

Six of the agents are "workers" and one is a "manager". Each gets its own tmux window. Here is a screenshot of me talking to the manager.

On the left is Claude code (any of the agent harnesses can be the manager at any given time)

On the right you can see a run of the local-step command, which prompts each worker according to a deterministic state machine.

Currently all of the workers are in the IDLE state, except jc0, which is READY with a new plan to tackle something related to one of the open sorrows. I'll talk about this plan (which is stupid) in another post, in a bit.

The state machine is run by scripts in the scialect repo, which also includes the current prompts I'm using to guide different actions.

The main reason for moving the tools to a separate repo is that each worker has its own working copy of the JacobianChallenge project, and I didn't want to have to tell each worker to cherry pick changes every time I change a prompt. Instead, every step knows what prompts it uses, and those get copied to a local .sci/ directory that is listed in .gitignore.

The file docs/state-machine.md describes the current state machine. (The actual code is elsewhere, in typescript).

There is also some support for fanning out to control multiple Claude-code-in-the-cloud instances through browser automation, but I haven't used this much, as most of the problems I'm encountering have to do with project management (not math, not compute resources) and adding more workers simply doesn't help.

The main reason I stopped using Aristotle was just the slow turnaround time. Sometimes it starts working very quickly, but sometimes a task sits in a queue for hours, and there's no way to pay for priority.

Also, AFAIK, Aristotle is tied to version 4.28 of lean and Mathlib. This is not actually a problem, but at some point I had the (possibly mistaken) belief that getting comparator to run correctly would require upgrading the whole project. In any case, since I hadn't actually been using Aristotle for a while, I upgraded to lean v4.31.0-rc1, and have not tried using Aristotle since.

Is this actually an "autoformalization" ? (probably not)

I should note that everything is scialect is an evolving system... It's the result of me slowly moving my project management steps and manual prompts into reusable, scriptable chunks. I don't really know what rules make a good process, so I'm constantly tweaking them.

Before I had those scripts, I was manually writing prompts. I'm still manually write prompts, but more often now, they're "meta prompts" asking an agent to observe what's happening with the other agents, and diagnose what in the process went wrong.

On the other hand, I entered into this knowing nothing absolutely nothing about what the Jacobian is. So all the actual math is just coming directly out of the various AIs.

Almost everything committed up until now has been the result of top-down, stepwise refinement. I basically tell the AI to take the statement to formalize and phrase it in terms of other statements that it wishes it had. Those then become new sorry statements, and the process repeats recursively.

I only have a few hours a week to dedicate to this project, so I've tried to get the system to prompt itself and run autonomously. However, I check in on it briefly as it runs, restart it when it gets stuck, ask "why did you do <some stupid thing>", etc.

At the end, I do not expect to claim this is as a true"autoformalization", but my hope is that when I am done, I will be able to re-enter the challenge into a fresh copy of whatever the "scialect" repo turns into, and it will be able to complete the challenge autonomously, in a much shorter amount of time.

thanks for sharing your process, this is very interesting. Btw, the dep graph above is too low quality to read but https://tangentstorm.github.io/JacobianChallenge/blueprint/dep_graph_document.html has it zoomable. How stable would you say has the dep graph been vs changing as formalization hits some unforseen issue , i.e. you bubble down and then agents realize, oh I needed some other theory or my upstream definition was off which made it unusable.

current problem A: hardware constraints

One reason I have only 7 workers on my machine is that I only have room on my hard drive for 7 copies of the .lake cache for MathLib.

Today I learned that lake has support for sharing the cache between multiple working directories, and I am experimenting with taking advantage of that fact.

Even so, my top-down building approach means that I'm usually building new things in the leaves of the dependency graph, which means I am constantly changing things that break the local build cache, which means more time and more CPU to build the project.

Multiply this by several agents working in parallel, and I often find my machine reporting double-digit loads. The loads reported by uptime say 1.0 when the CPUs are at full utilization, and I often see loads like 19.x, 25.x, etc. when running.

On several occasions, I discovered that the entire machine (a slightly old M1 mac mini) had simply rebooted and the entire swarm had been dead for hours.

For what it's worth, there are numerous github "continuous integration" hooks set up, so that the web and PDF version(s) of the blueprints build on every push. Also the comparator runs, etc. So, one alternative to building locally is just to push to a branch and let github's machines handle it.

(I don't think anyone but me can see these, but I get little messages telling me what scripts have passed or failed. It seems something on the most recent push broke the comparator check):


Implementing from the bottom up would solve this problem and allow many more parallel workers on the same machine -- the changes would not lead to cascades of recompiles, and so merging could be an ongoing, extremely fast process.

However, adding more workers probably still wouldn't help at the moment, because the quality of the work itself is so bad, which I'll discuss in another post in a bit.

Rado Kirov said:

How stable would you say has the dep graph been vs changing as formalization hits some unforseen issue , i.e. you bubble down and then agents realize, oh I needed some other theory or my upstream definition was off which made it unusable.

This has happened several times. Here is a local copy of my current dependency graph, which is a perfect example:

The public version again:

I know it's too small to read. The details don't really matter.

Basically everything that's different between the thumbnails is that we picked one of the orange nodes (now purple to indicate we're focusing on it) and then added a bunch of blueprint nodes.

This is the new approach: build the blueprint from the top down, but keep going until all the leaves are existing, non-sorry, named statements either in MathLib or elsewhere in the project.

And hooray! We can build bottom-up! (For some reason this graph is built with the arrows pointing backwards and the root of the tree at the bottom, unlike normal trees which every child knows have their root at the top and leaves at the bottom. When I say "bottom-up" I mean going from existing mathlib statements toward the 24 sorrows in Challenge.lean)

The agent working on this branch took most of the past two days to build that graph, and at some point, we started assigning other workers to help it - so for the first time, it was a "team effort" all working up to one intermediate statement.

... Except there's still one orange sorry left:

Here's what's wrong (quoting the current mgr worker):

  • The genus-0 proof had to produce a biholomorphism X ≅ sphere (#232/#233).
  • But its "supporting" lemmas built their inputs by assuming that biholomorphism already exists.
  • So the proof used its own conclusion as a premise — circular.

Frustrating.

(Apparently some of the green nodes are "real" math work and the whole graph doesn't have to be scrapped, but...)

Another example is https://github.com/tangentstorm/JacobianChallenge/issues/244 , which is basically that we're relying on a statement that is false as stated. (The idea is true, but the actual statement has problems...)

This is the inherent danger of the top-down approach. It's also very frustrating to have a graph that looks like it's just about done, only to find out that one leaf is a "genuine mathematical gap -- months of effort".

The bottom-up "danger" is more like wasting time proving (or failing to prove) statements you don't need.

At one point, there was a whole section of the blueprint called "analytical gaps" which included several chapters of generic analytical topics that the system at the time was certain we were going to need. Many of those statements are still in the repo, formalized or stated in Lean, but not actually reachable from lake build Jacobian/Solution.lean.

Basically at no point so far have I had any issue with the AIs not "understanding the math" or not knowing what needs to be done. They can explain any and all parts of the math content, and when they check each others work, they all agree on the ideas.

But I've struggled to get the agents to reconcile what they "know" (the math ideas) with what they're doing (the actual formalization steps).

Unfortunately, I have learned what a Jacobian is

I have deliberately tried to stay mostly ignorant of the mathematical content of this project. If it's truly an auto formalization, it really shouldn't be asking anyone else's advice about the math.

It's bad enough that I'm currently acting like a project manager. But that's unavoidable because I don't yet have a good, automated process for formalizing mathematics - at least not on this scale.

Ideally, there'd be a system that handles the generic process of formalizing mathematics, and the AI agents would follow that process to weave the informal math knowledge from their training into nice formalized lean statements...

My role is to "fill in" for this generic process, until the system does it for me.

I had already made a few concessions, by adding the "plain English" bits to the blueprint and resulting PDF. That's fine, but then of course I read them... Luckily, they're not yet all that informative -- I told the agents to basically write a very high level overview of things that convey the basic idea. I specifically referenced the style of Quanta magazine in the prompt. (I don't think it reached that level of quality)

But today I broke down and had a long conversation with Claude, getting it to really explain the ideas to me.

It's not that I wanted to know. It's that I can't seem to figure out how to get the agents to clearly state where the formalization needs to start. Basically, I can't switch over to working bottom-up because I have no clue where the bottom is, and the agents won't tell me. Every proposed leaf turns out to be "a genuine mathlib gap -- months of work".

I asked it to assume I'm a high school student that knows nothing past calculus, and try to get me to the Jacobian as quickly as possible.

It seems to be hard for the AI to do this, and it's still hard for me to retroactively find the beginning.

If you think of the Jacobian as a function, then basically you plug in a Riemann surface of genus g and you get back a torus of complex dimension g.

Example: a sphere is a Riemann surface of dimension 0, and its Jacobian is a single point (torus of complex dimension 0). "Genus" is not yet defined in mathlib (it means the number of holes in the surface)... And so part of the challenge is to define what genus is. It would be easy to just define genus = 0, which is why there's a specific "anti-hack" line in the challenge file to prevent this.

Anyway, a more interesting case is a genus 1 Riemann surface. 1 hole, so the famous donut and/or coffee-mug (or rather the surface thereof). Its Jacobian is a torus.

I previously thought of the donut itself (or at least its surface) as a torus. Like in my head it's a 2d surface embedded in a 3d world. But we don't care about the 3d world. It's really more like the pac-man world: a single flat sheet, but it wraps around in 2 different ways.

A "double donut" (like a donut that's a figure 8) has 2 holes -> genus 2. So its Jacobian is a complex torus of dimension 2. That means each point has 2 complex coordinates... Which I think most non-mathematicians would just call a "4-dimensional space".

Anyway, I'm not going to embarrass myself further and try to explain all the details I learned, but that's a start.

Now, how do you actually specify the g-complex-dimensional torus? How do you even express the idea of mapping a surface to a space (in lean)?

And from a learner's point of view, why would you even want to?

Why would you take step 0?

Like pedagogically, you want the teacher to give the student some problem to think about to motivate constructing this complex torus (ex: the Jacobian of an elliptic curve reveals lots of neat properties like the fact that when a line intersects 3 points on the curve, those points sum to 0), but in a formalization process, the motivation is just an irrelevant side quest. (Or perhaps it's a potential test case?)

Like I think the planning process really needs to be a sort of back and forth where you work bottom up and top down....

And maybe part of the elicitation process ought to be having one "student agent" asking "why?" and "what is this?" and "where is this in lean?" and then getting a "teacher agent" to explain it... just to map out the actual dependency graph.

... I think at this point I'm just rambling now, so I will stop.

I think that your abstract suspense comes from the fact that your only motivation is to complete the formalization. Now, if you instead came to this from an open problem the proof of which may require this formalization (or even only having all statements as correct axioms with literature references) ...
